landmarks.name: Phoenix Islands Protected Area
landmarks.writeup: One of the largest marine protected areas in the world, known for its rich biodiversity and pristine coral reefs.

wiki.extract: The Phoenix Islands Protected Area (PIPA) is located in the Republic of Kiribati, an ocean nation in the central Pacific approximately midway between Australia and Hawaii. PIPA constitutes 11.34% of Kiribati's exclusive economic zone (EEZ), and with a size of 408,250 km2 (157,630 sq mi), it is one of the largest marine protected areas (MPA) and one of the largest protected areas of any type on Earth. The PIPA was also designated as the world's largest and deepest UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2010.

landmarks.name: Betio War Memorial
landmarks.writeup: A memorial on Tarawa Atoll commemorating those who died in World War II during the Battle of Tarawa.

wiki.extract: Tarawa is an atoll and the capital of the Republic of Kiribati, in the Micronesia region of the central Pacific Ocean. It comprises North Tarawa, which has 6,629 inhabitants and much in common with other more remote islands of the Gilbert group, and South Tarawa, which has 56,388 inhabitants as of 2015, half of the country's total population. The atoll was the site of the Battle of Tarawa during World War II.

landmarks.name: Te Umanibong Museum
landmarks.writeup: The national museum located in South Tarawa, showcasing Kiribati's cultural heritage and history.

wiki.extract: Te Umanibong or the Kiribati Cultural Museum, or Kiribati Museum and Cultural Centre, is a museum in Bikenibeu on the atoll of Tarawa in Kiribati. It displays artefacts and other items of cultural and historic significance.

cultural_events.name: Te Kaimatoa
cultural_events.writeup: A traditional dance festival celebrating Kiribati culture, featuring music, dance, and storytelling.

wiki.extract: Kiribati, officially the Republic of Kiribati, is an archipelagic country spanning the Micronesia and Polynesia sub-regions of Oceania in the central Pacific Ocean. The state comprises 32 atolls and other islands and one remote raised coral island, Banaba. Its total land area is 811 km2 (313 sq mi) dispersed over 3,441,810 km2 (1,328,890 sq mi) of ocean. The spread of the country's islands, from Banaba in the west to Kiritimati in the east straddles the equator and the 180th meridian. The International Date Line goes around Kiribati and swings far to the east, almost reaching 150°W. This brings Kiribati's easternmost islands, the southern Line Islands south of Hawaii, into the same day as the Gilbert Islands and places them in the most advanced time zone on Earth: UTC+14.

cultural_events.name: Independence Day
cultural_events.writeup: Celebrated on July 12th, marking Kiribati's independence from the United Kingdom in 1979.

wiki.extract: Independence Day is celebrated annually on 15 August as a public holiday in India commemorating the nation's independence from the United Kingdom on 15 August 1947. On this day the Indian Independence Act 1947 came into effect, transferring legislative sovereignty to the Indian Constituent Assembly. India attained independence following the independence movement noted for largely non-violent resistance and civil disobedience led by the Indian National Congress under the leadership of Mahatma Gandhi.

food_writeup: Kiribati cuisine primarily consists of seafood, coconut, breadfruit, and pandanus. Traditional dishes often include fish prepared with coconut milk and root crops.
brief_history: Kiribati was first settled by Micronesian peoples around 3000 years ago. It became a British protectorate in the late 19th century and gained independence in 1979. The country faces significant challenges due to climate change and rising sea levels.

current_conflicts: Kiribati faces no active military conflicts but is significantly impacted by climate change, leading to environmental and socio-economic challenges.

commentary.inflation_management: Kiribati uses the Australian dollar, so it has no monetary policy at all - inflation is whatever Australia and world food-fuel prices deliver. The result is extreme volatility for a micro-economy: 13.7% in 2008, deflation of -3.9% in 2010, -3% in 2012, then 9.8% in 2009 and 9.3% in 2023 on global shocks. The IMF projects 6.5% for 2025, still elevated. Price stability is structurally impossible to manage domestically; the only buffers are fiscal - the Revenue Equalization Stabilization Fund and fishing-license windfalls that let the government smooth household costs through subsidies when import prices spike.
commentary.debt_management: Kiribati barely borrows: gross debt peaked at 21.2% of GDP in 2016 and has fallen to a projected 8% in 2025, the series low. The fiscal story is the opposite of most Pacific islands - tuna fishing-license revenues under the Vessel Day Scheme turned the budget structurally strong through the 2010s, and the RERF sovereign wealth fund (built from earlier phosphate wealth) provides a cushion worth several times GDP. Debt sustainability is not the question; the question is whether fishing revenues, which depend on tuna migration patterns shifting with ocean warming, hold up.

key_events.event: September: switched diplomatic recognition from Taiwan to China, deepening Beijing's Pacific footprint.
President Maamau re-elected in June, consolidating the pro-China foreign policy turn.
Reopened the Phoenix Islands Protected Area to commercial fishing, trading conservation for revenue.
COVID-19 arrived after a long virus-free stretch, ending one of the world's strictest border closures.

commentary.outlook_next_decade: Kiribati's finances are the strongest in the Pacific on paper, but the economy is an existential bet on sea-level rise: much of the country sits under two meters above the ocean. Fishing revenues should stay strong near-term, funding adaptation and the RERF. The strategic risk is geopolitical - Kiribati's location and its China ties make it a pawn in great-power competition, which could either bring investment or instability. Macroeconomically, the decade looks stable; physically, it is the most threatened nation on earth.
commentary.caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
